title: 3 human cases of avian flu confirmed in Washington state, including a death: WHO
summary: The World Health Organization said on Tuesday it had been notified by the United States of three confirmed human cases of bird flu in Washington state, including one death.

image.caption: Three cases of bird flu among humans have been confirmed in Washington state, including one death. Officials say all three were adults who worked on dairy farms in a region where bird flu in cattle was recently detected. (Annie Rice/Reuters)

blocks.text: The World Health Organization said on Tuesday it had been notified by the United States of three confirmed human cases of bird flu in Washington state, including one death.
All worked on dairy farms in county where bird flu was recently detected in cattle
All three cases were adults who worked on dairy farms in the state's Yakima County, where the avian influenza virus was recently detected in cattle, the WHO said.
The UN agency said there was no evidence so far of human-to-human transmission based on information available.

The first patient developed mild symptoms, including eye irritation and a runny nose, and was not hospitalized. The second, who had underlying medical conditions, developed severe respiratory illness and died on Nov. 1. The third developed conjunctivitis and recovered without hospitalization.
Genetic sequencing confirmed all three infections were caused by the H5N1 virus, with strains closely matching those detected in dairy cattle in Washington.
H5N1 bird flu is a subtype of influenza A virus that primarily infects wild and domestic birds, and occasionally spreads to mammals, including humans.
A researcher uses a pipette to transfer a sample into a microtube as researchers work to monitor avian influenza, at the Institut Pasteur in Paris, on Nov. 24. (Gonzalo Fuentes/Reuters)

While the current public health risk is low, the U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is watching the situation carefully and working with states to monitor people with animal exposures.
The CDC has reported 75 human H5 infections since February 2024, including the three cases in Washington.
Canada has never recorded a case of avian flu in the dairy industry, but officials in British Columbia are monitoring the situation directly south of them.
Dr. Theresa Burns, B.C.'s chief veterinarian, said earlier this week that all cattle imported from the U.S. are tested and tracked, and that it’s mandatory to report infected livestock.

No human cases of avian flu have been reported in Canada since a B.C. teenager contracted the virus in 2024 and suffered serious illness before recovering. But avian flu among poultry flocks has seen an increase this month in the wake of a national poultry show. As of last Thursday, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency had confirmed 11 cases of the avian flu connected to the Canadian National Poultry Show held on Nov. 7 in Moose Jaw.
